title: Fish & Seafood Markets in the US
one_liner: Specialty fish markets remain a fragmented fresh-seafood retail niche where premium service and local sourcing offset pressure from supermarkets, clubs and online seafood sellers.
overview: This industry covers brick-and-mortar specialty retailers that primarily sell fresh, frozen, cured and prepared fish and seafood directly to consumers and some food-service buyers; supermarket seafood counters and pure online seafood sales are excluded in the baseline definition. The business is mature, local and highly fragmented, with revenue driven by fresh product availability, consumer confidence in seafood quality, disposable income, restaurant demand and the ability to explain origin, freshness, preparation and sustainability. Compared with supermarkets and warehouse clubs, specialty operators compete less on price and more on freshness, service, variety, local species and prepared seafood.

key_stats.market_size: $3.3 billion revenue in 2024 for US fish and seafood markets; 2025 modeled run-rate about $3.4 billion if 2024 specialty-channel revenue rises with 2025 industry inflation assumptions.
key_stats.growth: 5.4% annual growth over 2022-2024 reported for the sector; 2025 specialty-channel nominal growth is likely low-single-digit as price gains offset flat-to-declining volumes.
key_stats.profit_margin: 4.9% EBIT margin in 2022 baseline; 2025 margins are pressured by labor, rent, freight, shrink and import costs but supported by premium fresh seafood pricing.
key_stats.establishments: 4,394 establishments in 2022 baseline; 2027 baseline forecast was 4,549 establishments.
key_stats.enterprises: 4,339 enterprises in 2022 baseline, indicating very low concentration.
key_stats.employment: 14,783 employees in 2022 baseline; 2027 baseline forecast was 15,796 employees.
key_stats.consumer_consumption: 19.1 pounds per capita US seafood consumption in 2023, NOAA's latest published annual consumption figure as of 2026.
key_stats.imports: 80% of seafood eaten by Americans in 2023 came from foreign imports, according to NOAA.
key_stats.retail_price_signal: Fresh, frozen and shelf-stable seafood averaged more than $10 per pound in December 2025 in Circana retail data cited by The National Provisioner.
key_stats.fresh_retail_context: Fresh seafood sales were $744 million in December 2025 across Circana MULO+ retail channels, while full-year 2025 fresh seafood dollars rose but pounds fell 0.5% versus 2024.

baseline_2022.growth: 5.5% revenue growth in 2022 and 4.3% annualized growth over 2017-2022.
baseline_2022.product_mix: Fresh finfish 55.0%, fresh shellfish 35.8%, prepared fish 3.5%, frozen seafood 2.7% and other 3.0% of 2022 revenue.

how_it_makes_money: Operators buy seafood from fishermen, aquaculture producers, processors and wholesalers, then mark up fresh finfish, shellfish, frozen seafood, cured seafood, prepared seafood and complementary items. Revenue is concentrated in fresh salmon, tuna, cod, tilapia, shrimp, oysters, clams, crab and lobster, with higher margins coming from premium species, filleting, custom cuts, prepared meals, party trays, local catch, sustainability-certified products and knowledgeable service.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline points to a labor-intensive specialty retail model: wages were $417 million, or about 11.3% of 2022 revenue, and EBIT profit was 4.9%. The largest cost is seafood inventory purchases, followed by wages for skilled counter staff and cutters, rent for high-traffic retail locations, utilities and refrigeration, packaging, spoilage and shrink, freight, insurance, marketing, card fees and compliance. In 2025, cost pressure increased from higher import duties, higher shellfish prices, freight volatility and wage competition, while premium pricing helped protect gross margin for operators with differentiated fresh supply.
major_players: Independent fishmongers and neighborhood seafood markets
Regional specialty seafood retailers and public-market vendors
Restaurant-adjacent seafood markets and prepared-seafood counters
Competitive set: supermarkets and grocery chains with seafood counters
Competitive set: Costco, Walmart, warehouse clubs and supercenters
Competitive set: online direct-to-consumer seafood sellers
current_dynamics: The specialty channel is recovering unevenly after the 2022 rebound. Higher seafood prices lift nominal revenue but also push budget-sensitive shoppers toward supermarkets, warehouse clubs, frozen seafood and shelf-stable options. Salmon is the strongest fresh-species anchor in 2025 retail data, while shellfish, especially crab and some shrimp demand, has been weaker because price jumps hurt volume. Import reliance keeps supply exposed to tariffs, MMPA admissibility rules and documentation requirements. FDA traceability compliance was delayed from January 20, 2026 toward July 20, 2028 enforcement timing, reducing near-term compliance pressure but keeping traceability investment on the agenda.
whats_growing: Fresh salmon, value-added and prepared seafood, tinned and shelf-stable seafood, transparent sourcing, local and domestic catch positioning, aquaculture-backed supply, loyalty-driven specialty retail, chef-style meal solutions and premium products for higher-income shoppers are growing. Circana data cited for 2025 showed salmon fresh/refrigerated retail sales of $4.1 billion, up 5.8% in dollars and 2.4% in pounds, while shelf-stable seafood reached $3.4 billion from December 2024 through December 2025, up 2% in dollars and 1% in units.
whats_shrinking: Undifferentiated fresh fish markets, price-led commodity shellfish, crab volume, some shrimp momentum in late 2025, low-service counters, stores without reliable sourcing stories and operators unable to manage shrink are under pressure. Circana data cited for 2025 showed fresh seafood pounds down 0.5% versus 2024 and shellfish pound sales declining by roughly 8% to 10% year over year in multiple quarters through 2025.
recent_developments: 2025: ResearchAndMarkets reported US fish and seafood markets revenue of $3.3 billion in 2024 and 5.4% annual growth over 2022-2024.
2025: US seafood import duties reached $2.24 billion, with an 8.43% average duty rate on import value, according to Mississippi State Extension analysis.
Sept. 2, 2025: NOAA announced 2025 MMPA comparability determinations, with certain fish products from denied foreign fisheries prohibited from US import beginning Jan. 1, 2026.
Dec. 2025: Circana data cited by The National Provisioner showed seafood prices averaging more than $10 per pound and fresh seafood sales of $744 million for the month.
Feb. 19, 2026: FDA issued additional Food Traceability Rule guidance and continued implementation engagement after proposing a 30-month compliance-date extension in 2025.
Mar. 3, 2026: NOAA updated Fisheries of the United States with 2023 consumption of 19.1 pounds per capita and 80% import reliance.
outlook: Through 2026, specialty fish markets should see modest nominal growth rather than broad volume growth. Price inflation, premium salmon, prepared seafood and health positioning support revenue, but high prices, tariffs, consumer trade-down and supermarket competition limit traffic. The strongest operators will use traceability, local supply, staff expertise, prepared-food convenience and restaurant-quality merchandising to justify price premiums. The weakest stores will be squeezed by shrink, labor costs and commodity seafood that shoppers can buy more cheaply elsewhere. The baseline 2022 forecast of $4.0 billion by 2027 still looks possible only for well-positioned specialty operators if price gains and premium mix continue, but 2024 third-party revenue of $3.3 billion suggests the channel has not fully sustained the 2022 rebound.

title: Foot Care Product Manufacturing
one_liner: A small, fragmented US manufacturing niche making OTC and medical foot treatments, braces, pads, insoles, creams, powders and filers.
overview: US manufacturers make medicated and nonmedicated foot-care preparations and light devices for dry skin, athlete's foot, cracked heels, blisters, corns, calluses, bunions, arch support and heel pain. Baseline IBIS data showed 2021 revenue of $633.2 million and a 2021-2026 forecast of $673.0 million, implying a 2026 manufacturing market near $673.0 million. The demand pool is larger than domestic manufacturing because 2021 domestic demand was $1.021 billion and 2021 imports were $575.0 million. Current 2025-2026 demand indicators are favorable: Census reported 61.2 million Americans age 65 and older in 2024, CDC reported 40.1 million Americans with diabetes in 2026, and global foot-care product researchers estimate faster growth in consumer foot treatments than in the US manufacturing base.

key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 forecast CAGR: 1.2%; 2026 estimated annual growth: about 1.2%
key_stats.consumer_market_context: 2025 global foot-care products market: $11.5 billion; 2026 global estimate: $12.2 billion; 2026-2033 CAGR: 6.8%; 2025 North America share: 34.3%
key_stats.demographic_demand: 2024 US age 65-plus population: 61.2 million; 2026 CDC diabetes estimate: 40.1 million people

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimate: $640.8 million US manufacturer revenue, derived from 2021 $633.2 million and the 2021-2026 1.2% CAGR baseline forecast
baseline_2022.imports: 2022 implied baseline trajectory: imports near $574.4 million if 2021-2026 import CAGR of -0.1% held
baseline_2022.exports: 2022 implied baseline trajectory: exports near $190.6 million if 2021-2026 export CAGR of 1.7% held
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022 implied baseline trajectory: about 5.1%-5.2%, moving from 2021 5.1% toward 2026 5.3%

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling branded and private-label foot creams, antifungal and wart treatments, powders, pads, sleeves, braces, insoles, heel lifts, pumice stones and filers to drugstores, mass merchants, e-commerce retailers, medical-supply wholesalers and export distributors. Value is created through formulation, FDA OTC compliance where relevant, packaging, brand trust, retail placement and product claims tied to comfort, pain relief, fungal treatment, diabetic foot care or cosmetic foot wellness.
cost_structure: The 2021 baseline margin was 5.1%, with 2026 forecast margin at 5.3%. Major costs are chemical and active ingredients for creams and antifungals, textiles, foams, gels, adhesives and plastics for pads and insoles, packaging, outsourced or domestic production labor, quality and regulatory compliance, retailer slotting and trade promotion, freight, warehousing and marketing. Import-heavy segments such as filers, low-priced pads and some insoles face 2025-2026 tariff and landed-cost volatility, while branded medical and treatment products have more pricing power.
major_players: Scholl's Wellness Company / Dr. Scholl's: leading branded insoles, foot-care treatments and international Scholl products; 2021 acquisition created a global foot-care platform with more than $700 million in annual retail sales at that time
Gold Bond / Chattem / Sanofi retained Gold Bond LLC: major US foot powder and skin-care brand, with 2025-2026 ownership and manufacturing arrangements affected by the Sanofi-Opella separation
Advantice Health / Kerasal: cracked-heel, foot-repair and nail-care products, with 2025 US trademark activity and 2025 Canada patch launch
Bayer HealthCare: Lotrimin and Tinactin antifungal products, including 2025 DailyMed labeling for Tinactin
Karo Healthcare / Lamisil: global OTC antifungal brand acquired from Haleon in 2023, with 2022 Lamisil topical net sales of EUR 65 million disclosed at deal announcement
Smaller private-label and contract manufacturers: fragmented producers of creams, pads, braces, insoles, powders and filers serving mass retail, pharmacy and e-commerce channels
current_dynamics: The industry is steadier than fashion footwear because many products address recurring pain, fungal infections, cracked skin and diabetic foot risks, but domestic manufacturing growth is modest because imports already served 56.3% of 2021 domestic demand. In 2025-2026, aging and diabetes support medical and preventive foot-care demand, e-commerce expands discovery for branded treatments, and premium insoles are moving toward performance and sports positioning. Offsetting pressures include private-label competition, mass-retailer bargaining power, China-linked sourcing exposure, higher tariff pass-through in 2025 retail goods, and a mature domestic customer base.
whats_growing: Treatment-oriented and wellness-positioned products are growing fastest: 2025 global foot treatments held 42.8% of the global foot-care products market; 2026-2033 US foot-care products CAGR is estimated at 5.5% by Grand View Research. Products tied to aging, diabetes foot checks, cracked heels, fungal infections, nail appearance, athletic performance and premium insoles are better positioned than basic commodity filers. E-commerce and pharmacy channels remain important, with 2025 global pharmacy and drugstore share at 37.9%.
whats_shrinking: Domestic production of low-priced commodity goods such as pumice stones, foot filers, simple pads and some insoles is structurally weaker because imports captured a large share of domestic demand by 2021. The 2021 baseline put pumice stones and other foot filers at only 2.7% of industry revenue, and insoles and heel lifts at 15.6% after production shifted abroad. Operator count is also shrinking, from 114 enterprises in 2021 to a 2026 forecast of 108 enterprises.
recent_developments: June 2026: Census released Vintage 2025 population files, following 2024 estimates that put the US age 65-plus population at 61.2 million, a demand tailwind for foot-care products.
May 20, 2026: Scholl's Wellness Company, parent of Dr. Scholl's, acquired VKTRY, adding premium carbon-fiber performance insoles to its foot-care platform.
March 16, 2026: CDC reported 40.1 million people with diabetes in the US, reinforcing medical demand for preventive foot checks, fungal treatments and protective foot products.

March 5, 2026: Federal Reserve research found 2025 tariff pass-through of at least 30% for China-origin retail goods by December 2025, raising landed-cost pressure for import-exposed foot-care categories.
June 9, 2025: Kerasal launched Nighttime Renewal Nail Patches in Canada, extending foot and nail care into patch-format self-care products.
April 30, 2025: Sanofi completed the Opella consumer-health separation, while Sanofi's 2025 SEC filing stated Gold Bond product-range sales continued in the US through retained Gold Bond LLC.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is stable but not high growth. Manufacturer revenue is best framed near the baseline 2026 estimate of $673.0 million, with roughly 1.2% annualized growth from 2021. Demand should be supported by 2024-2026 aging and diabetes data, physician utilization, OTC self-care routines and premium performance insoles. Margin expansion is limited because retailers and imports pressure prices, while tariffs and freight volatility can raise costs. The most defensible operators will own brands, differentiated formulations, APMA or clinical credibility, e-commerce execution, and higher-value insoles or treatment products rather than commodity accessories.

title: Footwear Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: A mature footwear distribution channel is being squeezed between import-cost volatility, cautious consumers and brands rebuilding selective wholesale partnerships after years of DTC expansion.
overview: The industry remains a large but slow-growth wholesale trade market tied to consumer footwear demand, retailer inventory cycles and imported shoe costs. The 2022 IBIS baseline showed revenue of $32.825 billion after a 2020 COVID shock and a 2017-2022 CAGR of -3.9%, with wholesalers losing share as Nike, Adidas and other brands sold more directly to consumers and retailers. Current 2025-2026 indicators point to stabilization rather than a clean rebound: 2025 personal spending on footwear was about $121 billion, 2025 US footwear imports were 2.015 billion pairs, and 2026 retail footwear dollars are being supported more by price than by unit growth. The channel is still relevant because major brands need wholesale partners for reach, replenishment and inventory normalization, but margin risk is elevated because tariffs, freight, markdowns and consumer price resistance are harder for wholesalers to pass through.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated US footwear wholesaling revenue: about $35 billion, using the 2023 IBIS-reported $35.7 billion industry revenue base and 2025-2026 low-growth retail/trade indicators.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated industry revenue growth: roughly flat to +1%; 2026 demand indicators remain low-growth, with Q1 2026 US footwear retail dollar sales +1% year over year and units down.
key_stats.imports: 2025 US footwear imports: 2.015 billion pairs; about 99% of shoes sold in the US were imported.
key_stats.import_value: 2025 US footwear imports: about $26.6 billion for HS 64 footwear.
key_stats.consumer_spending: 2025 US personal spending on footwear: about $121 billion.
key_stats.retail_sales: May 2026 US shoe-store retail sales: $3.339 billion, not seasonally adjusted.
key_stats.prices: June 2026 footwear import price index: 122.8, 2000=100; June 2026 CPI-U footwear index: 151.231, 1982-84=100.
key_stats.profitability: 2022 baseline profit: $1.641 billion, equal to a 5.0% EBIT margin.

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue mix: women's and girls' non-athletic footwear 62.6%, men's and boys' non-athletic footwear 25.0%, athletic footwear 9.5%, infants' footwear and accessories 2.9%.
baseline_2022.downstream_mix: 2022 downstream retail markets generated 72.3% of industry revenue.

how_it_makes_money: Wholesalers earn gross margin by sourcing footwear from manufacturers, licensed brands and importers, holding or arranging inventory, selling assortments to retail and e-commerce accounts, and providing replenishment, sales representation, credit, warehousing, compliance and logistics services. Larger brand-owned wholesale arms also monetize access to high-demand product allocations, while independent distributors compete on niche brands, regional coverage, speed to market and service for retailers too small to buy efficiently from overseas factories or global brands directly.
cost_structure: The largest 2025-2026 cost bucket is merchandise purchases, especially imported footwear exposed to factory prices, ocean freight, tariffs and currency shifts. The 2022 baseline shows wages of $2.398 billion, or about 7.3% of 2022 revenue, and EBIT profit of $1.641 billion, or 5.0% of 2022 revenue. Other recurring costs include warehousing, freight, sales commissions, retailer chargebacks, inventory markdowns, technology, insurance, rent and financing costs for working capital. Tariff and freight volatility in 2025-2026 raises the risk that purchase-cost inflation arrives before wholesalers can reprice retailer contracts.
major_players: {'name': 'Nike Inc.', 'position': 'Major athletic-footwear brand and wholesale supplier; fiscal 2026 North America sales to wholesale customers were $11.958 billion, up 14% from fiscal 2025, while North America footwear revenue was $13.317 billion, up 5%.'}

{'name': 'Adidas AG / Adidas America', 'position': 'Major athletic and sport-lifestyle footwear wholesaler; 2025 global wholesale net sales were €14.833 billion and grew 12% currency-neutral for the Adidas brand, while 2025 North America Adidas-brand sales grew 10% currency-neutral excluding Yeezy.'}

{'name': 'Caleres Inc.', 'position': 'Branded footwear and retail operator with wholesale-facing Brand Portfolio; fiscal 2025 net sales were $2.758 billion, and Brand Portfolio net sales increased 7.3%, including the 2025 Stuart Weitzman acquisition.'}

{'name': 'Fragmented independent distributors', 'position': 'The 2022 baseline characterized the industry as low-concentration, with many small operators serving local retailers, niche brands, work footwear, fashion footwear and specialty channels.'}
current_dynamics: The market is being pulled in two directions in 2025-2026. Wholesale is gaining importance again for some brands that need retail partners to restore shelf presence and manage inventory, shown by Nike's fiscal 2026 North America wholesale rebound and Adidas's 2025 wholesale gains. At the same time, DTC, marketplaces and direct manufacturer relationships continue to cap wholesaler relevance. Demand is price-sensitive: 2026 retail footwear dollar growth is modest and unit growth is weak, so wholesalers are relying on athletic performance, running, comfort and back-to-school needs rather than broad discretionary strength. Tariffs are the main operating shock because imported footwear dominates US supply.
whats_growing: Performance and comfort-led categories are growing fastest. Circana reported Q1 2026 US footwear dollar sales +1%, performance footwear +5%, and running with double-digit dollar and unit growth. Running-inspired lifestyle silhouettes, sandals, slides, flip-flops, mules, clogs and ballerinas are also taking share where consumers see daily-use versatility. Wholesale partnerships with strong sell-through brands are improving as brands rebalance away from overly narrow DTC strategies.
whats_shrinking: Low-differentiation wholesale distribution is shrinking as brands and retailers transact directly, marketplace channels absorb demand, and retailers limit inventory risk. Fashion boots remained weak in Q1 2026, with ankle and mid-shaft softness outweighing gains in high-shaft styles. Athletic footwear spending faced pressure in 2025 consumer surveys, and price-sensitive households are trading down, delaying purchases or walking away from full-price shoes.
recent_developments: 2025-04-30: AlixPartners and FDRA reported that 78% of US shoppers had walked away from a footwear purchase because of cost.
2025-07-16: AlixPartners and FDRA reported that 80% of surveyed consumers expected to pay more for children's shoes for back-to-school 2025.
2026-04-09: FDRA-cited import data showed China supplied 964 million pairs of US footwear imports in 2025, with its share at a 35-year low.
2026-05-04: Circana reported Q1 2026 US footwear dollar sales +1% year over year, performance footwear +5%, and units down overall.
2026-07-10: FDRA warned that new tariffs, rising material costs and renewed freight pressure would shape the second half of 2026.
2026-07-17: FRED/BLS data showed the June 2026 footwear import price index at 122.8, up from 121.3 in December 2025.
outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is low-growth and margin-sensitive. Market size should hold near the mid-$30-billion range if footwear retail dollars remain positive, but real volume growth is likely limited by high prices and cautious household spending. Wholesalers with access to running, comfort, work/safety, children's and strong sport-lifestyle brands should outperform. Operators dependent on undifferentiated fashion shoes, weak brands or tariff-heavy sourcing lanes face higher markdown, financing and customer-concentration risk. The biggest upside is renewed brand use of wholesale partners to regain retail reach; the biggest downside is a tariff shock that wholesalers cannot pass through without losing orders.

title: For-Profit Universities in the US
one_liner: A regulated, adult-learner-focused higher education industry whose 2025 revenue recovered to about $13.6 billion while enrollment momentum weakened again in fall 2025.
overview: The industry consists of proprietary degree-granting colleges and universities that offer associate, bachelor's, master's and doctoral programs, often online or hybrid, and typically serve working adults, transfer students, military-affiliated learners and career changers. The 2022 baseline showed revenue of $12.519 billion after a 5.2% decline in 2022, while current market research cited 2025 for-profit university revenue of $13.6 billion. That implies a roughly 2.8% revenue CAGR from 2022 to 2025, but the operating environment is uneven: spring 2025 private for-profit baccalaureate undergraduate enrollment rose 3.3% to nearly 650,000, while final fall 2025 data showed private for-profit undergraduate enrollment down 2.0%. Large operators are concentrating around online scale, employer-funded enrollment, health professions, retention analytics and lower physical-campus exposure.

key_stats.growth: Estimated 2022-2025 revenue CAGR of about 2.8%, from $12.519 billion in 2022 to $13.6 billion in 2025
key_stats.enrollment: Nearly 650,000 private for-profit undergraduate students in spring 2025, up 3.3% from spring 2024; private for-profit undergraduate enrollment declined 2.0% in fall 2025

baseline_2022.growth: Revenue declined 5.2% in 2022 and grew at a 0.4% CAGR over 2017-2022
baseline_2022.profit: $1.940 billion in 2022 EBIT, equal to a 15.5% profit margin

how_it_makes_money: Operators primarily earn 2025 revenue from tuition and fees for accredited online, hybrid and campus-based degree programs. Federal Title IV student aid remains central to many schools' cash collection, while employer-paid and employer-discounted enrollment is increasingly important: University of Phoenix reported 32% of fiscal 2025 average degreed enrollment came through employer relationships, and Strategic Education reported employer-affiliated enrollment reached 31.2% of U.S. higher education enrollment in first-quarter 2025. Revenue is also earned from certificates, continuing education, corporate education partnerships and student-support services, though degree programs represented 97% of University of Phoenix fiscal 2025 net revenue.
cost_structure: Major 2025 costs include faculty and instructional delivery, student advising and career services, admissions and marketing, learning technology, compliance, financial-aid administration, accreditation, data security and remaining campus facilities. The 2022 baseline showed wages at $3.719 billion, equal to about 29.7% of 2022 revenue, and EBIT profit at 15.5% of 2022 revenue. Public-company segment data show the model can carry high operating leverage: Adtalem's fiscal 2025 cost of educational services was $771.4 million on $1.788 billion of revenue, while its fiscal 2025 segment adjusted operating income was $406.2 million; Strategic Education's 2025 U.S. higher education revenue was reported at $868.2 million; Perdoceo's 2025 enrollment growth required added marketing, admissions and student-support expense.

{'name': 'Phoenix Education Partners / University of Phoenix', 'position': 'Large online adult-learner university; fiscal 2025 net revenue was $1.007 billion and fiscal 2025 average total degreed enrollment was 81,900.'}

{'name': 'Strategic Education', 'position': 'Operator of Capella University and Strayer University; 2025 U.S. higher education enrollment was 85,306 students in the fall term and 2025 U.S. higher education revenue was reported at $868.2 million.'}

{'name': 'Perdoceo Education Corporation', 'position': 'Operator of Colorado Technical University, American InterContinental University System and University of St. Augustine; total student enrollment was 44,400 as of December 31, 2025, up 7.3% from December 31, 2024.'}

{'name': 'Grand Canyon Education', 'position': 'Education-services company tied to nonprofit university partners rather than a proprietary institution model; 2025 service revenue was $1.106 billion and partner enrollments were 136,239 as of December 31, 2025.'}
current_dynamics: In 2025-2026, demand is split between favorable adult-learner economics and tougher sector perception. Online universities retain advantages in flexibility, transfer-credit acceptance and working-adult scheduling, and health-care programs are benefiting from labor-market demand. At the same time, public and community colleges gained share in fall 2025, while private for-profit undergraduate enrollment declined 2.0%. Regulation is again a core strategic variable: Financial Value Transparency and Gainful Employment rules became effective July 1, 2024, student warnings and acknowledgements start July 1, 2026, and the July 1, 2026 STATS and Earnings Accountability final rule adds broader earnings-based Direct Loan risk across postsecondary programs.
whats_growing: Health professions, nursing, counseling, social work, medical support, employer-paid education benefits, transfer-friendly bachelor's completion, competency-based programs, AI-enabled student support, online graduate programs with clear occupational outcomes, and short certificate pathways tied to workforce demand are growing in 2025-2026. Adtalem's fiscal 2025 revenue grew 12.9% from fiscal 2024, University of Phoenix fiscal 2025 net revenue grew from $950.0 million in fiscal 2024 to $1.007 billion, and Perdoceo's total enrollment rose 7.3% in 2025.
whats_shrinking: Weak programs with poor debt-to-earnings or earnings-premium outcomes, legacy physical campuses, high-pressure lead-generation models, unaffiliated self-pay adult enrollment, and undifferentiated online bachelor's programs are shrinking or under pressure in 2025-2026. Final fall 2025 data showed private for-profit undergraduate enrollment down 2.0%, and 2025 enrollment reports showed computer and information science enrollment declining across award levels and institution types.
recent_developments: 2024-07-01: Financial Value Transparency and Gainful Employment regulations became effective for Title IV programs, with proprietary programs exposed to GE eligibility tests.
2025-01-15: National Student Clearinghouse reported fall 2024 postsecondary enrollment up 4.5%, with undergraduate enrollment up 4.7%.
2025-07-18: The U.S. Department of Education issued guidance implementing higher education provisions of the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including repayment and accountability changes.
2025-10-10: Phoenix Education Partners completed its IPO, after reporting fiscal 2025 University of Phoenix net revenue of $1.007 billion.
2026-01-15: National Student Clearinghouse final fall 2025 data showed total postsecondary enrollment up 1.0%, but private for-profit undergraduate enrollment down 2.0%.
2026-07-01: The Department of Education published the STATS and Earnings Accountability final rule, adding earnings benchmarks for Direct Loan eligibility.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive for revenue but cautious for enrollment quality and compliance risk. Revenue should be supported by tuition pricing, graduate health-care demand, employer-paid education benefits and online operating leverage, but broad growth is likely to trail public institutions unless for-profit operators can prove outcomes under the 2024-2026 earnings rules. The strongest operators in 2026 are those with high retention, employer channels, health-care program exposure, transparent pricing and low cohort-default or borrower-defense risk. Operators with weak graduate earnings, high federal-aid dependence or legacy recruiting liabilities face heightened program closures, teach-outs, regulatory costs and reputational drag.

title: Foreign Currency Exchange Services
one_liner: US foreign currency exchange services are rebounding unevenly as outbound travel and digital cross-border payments grow while inbound tourism and physical cash exchange remain below pre-pandemic norms.
overview: Foreign Currency Exchange Services covers nonbank currency dealers, exchange bureaus, travel-money providers and foreign-exchange technology platforms serving travelers, retailers, banks, credit unions and businesses. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline described a small, travel-sensitive US industry with $778.2 million of 2021 revenue, a 15.4% profit margin and a forecast recovery to roughly $1.3 billion by 2026. Current 2025-2026 data point to a slower, mixed recovery than that pre-2022 forecast: US outbound travel is above 2019 levels in many months, but inbound arrivals weakened during parts of 2025 and 2026, while consumer payment behavior continues shifting toward cards, mobile wallets, ACH and app-based cross-border transfers. Physical currency exchange remains most relevant at airports, tourist corridors, border markets, malls and for cash-preferring consumers, while growth is increasingly captured by omnichannel providers that combine online ordering, home delivery, institution-facing wholesale banknote services, compliance systems and international payment rails.

key_stats.market_size: $1.05 billion-$1.20 billion in US industry revenue, 2025 estimated from the 2021 IBISWorld $778.2 million baseline, current NTTO travel recovery data and public operator disclosures
key_stats.growth: 0% to 3% estimated US revenue growth in 2025, with outbound travel and digital payments offset by weaker inbound visitor volumes and pressure on retail cash exchange margins
key_stats.profit_margin: 15.4% in 2021 IBISWorld baseline; 2025 margins remain spread-sensitive and vary widely by airport rents, compliance cost and digital scale
key_stats.establishments: 420 establishments in 2021 IBISWorld baseline; 2025 footprint is more omnichannel, with CXI ending fiscal 2025 at 40 company-owned branches, 37 airport agent locations and OnlineFX home delivery in 46 states
key_stats.demand_driver_travel: 68.3 million total international visitors to the US in 2025 per NTTO's 2026-2030 forecast, rising to 70.5 million in 2026
key_stats.demand_driver_trade: US exports were $3.4323 trillion and imports were $4.3338 trillion in 2025, supporting corporate FX and cross-border payment demand
key_stats.payment_mix: Cash accounted for 14% of US consumer payments by number in 2024; the 2025 Survey and Diary found cash use in the prior 30 days declined from 83% of consumers in 2024 to 81% in 2025

baseline_2022.market_size: about $0.86 billion in 2022, estimated by applying the 2021 IBISWorld forecast path to the $778.2 million 2021 revenue baseline
baseline_2022.growth: about 10.9% in 2022 on the 2021 IBISWorld forecast path, reflecting expected post-COVID travel normalization
baseline_2022.context: The 2021 baseline forecast assumed revenue would rise at a 10.9% CAGR to $1.3 billion by 2026; current NTTO visitation data suggest the actual recovery has been more uneven.

how_it_makes_money: Bid-ask spreads on buying and selling foreign banknotes to travelers and businesses
Flat transaction fees, service fees and commissions on retail exchange orders
ATM withdrawal fees and currency-conversion margins at airport and tourist locations
Wholesale banknote supply and outsourcing contracts with banks, credit unions, airports and retailers
International payment and remittance fees, including FX margin on cross-border transfers
Prepaid travel-card issuance, reload and interchange-related economics where offered

largest_costs: Wages for branch, vault, customer support, treasury and compliance staff
Airport, mall and high-street rent or concession fees
Currency procurement, armored transport, vaulting, insurance and cash handling
Technology, cybersecurity, payment processing, bank connectivity and online-order infrastructure
Bank Secrecy Act, FinCEN, state licensing, OFAC, KYC and suspicious-activity monitoring compliance
Marketing, affiliate commissions and partner revenue shares
cost_structure.margin_pressure: Price comparison tools, bank/card no-FX-fee products and digital remittance apps compress consumer-facing spreads, while AML and licensing obligations keep fixed costs high.

major_players: Currency Exchange International (CXI)
Travelex
Wise US
Western Union
MoneyGram
OFX / Xe
Continental Currency Services and regional airport or tourist-market exchange bureaus
current_dynamics: Travel recovery is split: US outbound travel remains a tailwind for travel-money demand, while 2025-2026 inbound softness limits airport kiosk volumes in some corridors.
Digital providers are taking share from walk-up retail exchange by offering transparent fees, app-based transfers, multi-currency balances and home delivery.

Physical cash is no longer the primary US payment method, but it remains resilient enough to support niche exchange demand among tourists, older consumers, lower-income consumers, emergency users and cash-heavy destinations.
Airport locations still command convenience pricing, but they carry high concession and staffing costs and depend on passenger mix rather than total passenger counts alone.
Compliance is a central operating constraint because currency exchangers and many cross-border transfer providers are treated as money services businesses under FinCEN rules.

Corporate and financial-institution clients are increasingly important because wholesale banknote supply, international payments and embedded bank/credit-union FX can scale better than standalone kiosks.
whats_growing: Online foreign-currency ordering, home delivery and in-store pickup
Institution-facing foreign banknote services for banks and credit unions
Cross-border digital payments for consumers, freelancers and small businesses
Airport omnichannel models that combine ATMs, kiosks, mobile units and pre-order pickup
Compliance technology, transaction monitoring and identity verification
Outbound US leisure travel demand to Mexico, the Caribbean, Europe and Asia
whats_shrinking: Pure walk-up retail exchange branches away from high-tourism corridors
High-spread opaque pricing models as consumers compare rates online
Paper and cash share of everyday US payments, although cash has not disappeared
Traveler's checks and legacy prepaid products with weak mobile integration
Operators without scale to absorb licensing, AML, cybersecurity and banking-partner requirements
recent_developments: 2025-01: Travelex extended its Frankfurt Airport partnership for six years, underscoring the continued value of airport travel-money concessions.
2025-05: The CFPB amended its Wise order over remittance fee, exchange-rate and refund disclosures, highlighting fee-transparency risk for digital FX providers.
2025-10: FinCEN posted updated suspicious-activity reporting FAQs for MSBs, reinforcing compliance expectations for money services businesses.
2026-01: CXI reported fiscal 2025 revenue growth of 5% and net income of $10.3 million for the year ended October 31, 2025.
2026-07: The Federal Reserve's 2025 payments study reported 236.6 billion US noncash payments in 2024 and continued declines in check payments and ATM cash withdrawals.
2026-07: NTTO's 2026-2030 forecast projected total international visitation to the US at 68.3 million in 2025 and 70.5 million in 2026.
outlook: Through 2026-2030, US foreign currency exchange services should grow modestly rather than repeat the sharp rebound assumed in early post-pandemic forecasts. The strongest operators will look less like standalone exchange counters and more like regulated FX platforms with airport access, online ordering, bank partnerships, wholesale banknote logistics and digital international payments. Revenue growth should be helped by NTTO's forecast for US international visitation to rise from 68.3 million in 2025 to 85.2 million in 2030 and by continued expansion in cross-border commerce, but margins will remain constrained by transparent online pricing, no-FX-fee cards, digital wallet adoption, compliance costs and volatility in inbound tourism.
one_sentence: The industry earns spreads, fees and commissions from retail travel-money exchange, airport and mall kiosks, foreign-currency ATMs, wholesale banknote supply, international payments, prepaid travel cards and related remittance services.
